question: Which elements must a Texas notary seal contain?

options.text: A five-pointed star, the words "Notary Public, State of Texas", the notary's name, commission expiration date and notary ID number
options.why: Correct. These are the elements required by §406.013 and the Secretary of State's rules.

options.text: The notary's name, home address and county of residence
options.why: Wrong. Texas seals show neither an address nor a county.

options.text: The state flag, the notary's signature and bond number
options.why: Wrong. None of these is a required seal element.

options.text: The notary's name and the Secretary of State's signature
options.why: Wrong. The Secretary of State's signature isn't on the seal, and this leaves out the star, ID number and expiration date.

explanation: The Texas seal has a star of five points with "Notary Public, State of Texas" around it, plus the notary's name, commission expiration date and notary identification number.
source: Tex. Gov't Code §406.013; 1 Tex. Admin. Code ch. 87

question: Which of the following is NOT a required element of a Texas notary seal?

options.why: Correct (this is the element NOT required). Texas seals don't show a county; California's do.
Wrong. The name is required.
Wrong. The expiration date is required.
Wrong. The ID number assigned by the Secretary of State is required.

explanation: A current Texas seal does not show the county. Name, expiration date and ID number are required.

question: If a Texas notary seal is circular, what is its maximum diameter?

options.why: Correct. A circular seal may be no more than two inches in diameter.
Wrong. One inch is the width limit for a rectangular seal, not the circle's diameter.
Wrong. That's larger than allowed.
Wrong. The rule sets 2 inches as the maximum diameter.

explanation: A circular seal may be no more than two inches in diameter.
source: Tex. Gov't Code §406.013; 1 Tex. Admin. Code ch. 87

question: If a Texas notary seal is rectangular, what are its maximum dimensions?

options.why: Correct. That is the maximum rectangle the rule allows.
Wrong. That's too large in both dimensions.
Wrong. That exceeds both limits.
Wrong. A seal that size is allowed, but 1 × 1 isn't the maximum.

explanation: A rectangular seal may be no larger than one inch by two and one-half inches.
source: Tex. Gov't Code §406.013; 1 Tex. Admin. Code ch. 87

question: Which notarial acts must be authenticated with the notary's seal?

options.why: Correct. §406.013 requires the seal on all official acts.
Wrong. Jurats, oaths with certificates and other acts need the seal too.

options.text: Only acts for which a fee is charged
options.why: Wrong. Whether a fee is charged doesn't affect the seal requirement.

options.text: Only documents being sent out of state
options.why: Wrong. Documents used in Texas need the seal as well.

explanation: A notary must authenticate all official acts with the seal of office.

question: Who assigns the notary identification number shown on the seal?

options.why: Correct. The commissioning authority assigns the ID number.
Wrong. The surety issues a bond number, which isn't the notary ID.
Wrong. The vendor prints the number but doesn't assign it.
Wrong. County clerks have no role in Texas notary IDs.

explanation: The Secretary of State assigns each notary an identification number, which must appear on the seal.

question: Who may use a notary's official seal?

options.text: Only the notary to whom it was issued
options.why: Correct. The seal is personal to the commissioned notary.

options.text: Any notary in the same office
options.why: Wrong. Every notary must use their own seal with their own name and ID.

options.text: The notary's employer, when the notary is absent
options.why: Wrong. Even if the employer paid for it, the employer can't use the seal.

options.text: Any family member of the notary
options.why: Wrong. Anyone else using the seal is committing fraud.

explanation: The seal is the notary's personal official tool. No one else, including an employer, may use it.

question: The seal impression on a certificate should be:

options.text: Clear and legible enough to be photographically reproduced
options.why: Correct. Recording offices scan documents, so the impression must reproduce clearly.
Wrong. Covering signatures or text makes both illegible.
Wrong. An illegible seal can get the document rejected.
Wrong. Pencil isn't permanent and can't make a proper seal impression.

explanation: Documents are often recorded or scanned, so the impression must be clear enough to reproduce.

question: How should a notary sign a notarial certificate?

options.text: With their name exactly as it appears on the commission
options.why: Correct. A matching signature lets officials verify the commission.
Wrong. Initials make verification harder and aren't the commissioned name.
Wrong. A nickname doesn't match the official record.
Wrong. That would be forgery.

explanation: Signing exactly as commissioned lets anyone match the signature to the official record.

question: A notary is asked to sign and seal a blank certificate that the customer will fill in later. The notary should:

options.text: Refuse; certificates are completed only at the time of the notarial act
options.why: Correct. A pre-signed blank certificate can be attached to anything, which makes it a tool for fraud.

options.text: Agree if the customer is personally known
options.why: Wrong. Trusting the customer doesn't make a blank certificate true.
Wrong. There is no 'pending' notarial act.
Wrong. It's both a false certificate and an overcharge.

explanation: A pre-signed blank certificate invites fraud and makes a false certificate. It is misconduct.

question: After renewing a commission, why must a notary get a new seal?

options.text: The seal shows the commission expiration date, which changes
options.why: Correct. The old seal shows a date that is no longer accurate.

options.text: The old seal automatically becomes the state's property
options.why: Wrong. That isn't the reason; the problem is the outdated expiration date.

options.text: Seals must be replaced every year
options.why: Wrong. There's no annual replacement rule.

options.text: The notary ID number changes every term
options.why: Wrong. The ID number generally stays the same on renewal; the expiration date is what changes.

explanation: Because the expiration date is on the seal, a new commission requires a seal showing the new date.

question: The facts stated in a notarial certificate (date, venue, who appeared) must be:

options.why: Correct. The certificate is the notary's sworn-quality official statement.

options.text: Copied from the document's preparer without checking
options.why: Wrong. The notary is responsible for every fact in the certificate.
Wrong. The notary completes the certificate.
Wrong. An incomplete certificate is defective; if the facts aren't known, don't notarize.

explanation: A certificate is the notary's official statement. Knowingly stating false facts is misconduct and may be a crime.

question: What does the 'venue' portion of a certificate show?

options.text: The state and county where the notarial act took place
options.why: Correct. Venue is the location of the act, e.g. 'State of Texas, County of Travis'.
Wrong. The notary's address isn't part of the venue.

options.text: The county where the document will be recorded
options.why: Wrong. The recording location may differ from where the act took place.

options.text: The county where the notary's bond was filed
options.why: Wrong. Bond filing has nothing to do with venue.

explanation: Venue identifies where the notarization occurred, such as "State of Texas, County of Travis."

question: A document has no room for the notary's certificate and seal. What is the usual practice?

options.text: Attach a separate certificate securely to the document, identifying the document it belongs to
options.why: Correct. A loose certificate that describes the document (title, date, pages) can't easily be moved to another document.

options.text: Place the seal over the signer's signature
options.why: Wrong. That obscures the signature and the seal.

options.text: Notarize on the back of the signer's ID
options.why: Wrong. The certificate belongs with the document, not on an ID.
Wrong. The seal is required on every official act.

explanation: A loose certificate may be attached. It should identify the document so it can't be moved to another one.

question: When must a notary complete the certificate?

options.text: At the time of the notarial act, while the signer is present
options.why: Correct. Completing it on the spot keeps it accurate and prevents misuse.
Wrong. There's no after-the-fact window.
Wrong. Recording happens later and has nothing to do with the notary's act.

options.text: Whenever the signer asks for it
options.why: Wrong. A delayed certificate risks error and fraud.

explanation: Completing the certificate during the act keeps it accurate and prevents fraud.

question: A notary's commission has expired, but the old seal is still in the drawer. May the notary use it?

options.text: No; an expired notary may not perform notarial acts with any seal
options.why: Correct. Without a commission there's no authority, and the seal shows an expired date.
Wrong. The seal's condition doesn't grant authority.

options.text: Yes, if they cross out the expiration date
options.why: Wrong. Altering a seal impression is improper and still gives no authority.
Wrong. No exception lets an expired notary act.

explanation: With no active commission there is no authority to notarize, and the seal would show an expired date.
